```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::knit_hooks$set(small_mar = function(before, options, envir) {
  if (before) par(mar = c(3.4, 3.4, 0.6, 0.6), mgp = c(2.1, 0.6, 0))
})
knitr::opts_chunk$set(small_mar = TRUE)

library(bbmle)

occ <- read.csv("../data/class_examples/bobwhite_occupancy.csv")
counts <- read.csv("../data/class_examples/bobwhite_counts.csv")

pct <- function(x){ paste0(round(100 * x), "%") }
pct1 <- function(x){ paste0(sprintf("%.1f", 100 * x), "%") }

# the occupancy model, fitted the way students fit it
m_occ <- mle2(n_occupied ~ dbinom(size = n_routes, prob = plogis(a + b * elapsed)),
              start = list(a = 2, b = -0.05), data = occ)
a_hat <- coef(m_occ)["a"]
b_hat <- coef(m_occ)["b"]
ci_occ <- confint(m_occ)
se_occ <- sqrt(diag(vcov(m_occ)))
cor_ab <- cov2cor(vcov(m_occ))["a", "b"]

# occupancy in 2019, four ways
occ19_hat <- plogis(a_hat + 22 * b_hat)
corners <- expand.grid(a = ci_occ["a", ], b = ci_occ["b", ])
corners$p19 <- plogis(corners$a + 22 * corners$b)

set.seed(21)
draws <- MASS::mvrnorm(1000, mu = coef(m_occ), Sigma = vcov(m_occ))
occ19 <- plogis(draws[, "a"] + 22 * draws[, "b"])
occ19_ci <- quantile(occ19, c(0.025, 0.975))
obs19 <- occ$n_occupied[occ$year == 2019] / occ$n_routes[occ$year == 2019]

drop_draws <- plogis(draws[, "a"]) - occ19
drop_hat <- plogis(a_hat) - occ19_hat
drop_ci <- quantile(drop_draws, c(0.025, 0.975))

occ$from2019 <- occ$elapsed - 22
m_2019 <- mle2(n_occupied ~ dbinom(size = n_routes, prob = plogis(a + b * from2019)),
               start = list(a = 1, b = -0.05), data = occ)
rewrite_ci <- plogis(confint(m_2019, parm = "a"))

g19 <- function(th){ plogis(th[1] + 22 * th[2]) }
grad19 <- sapply(1:2, function(i){
  d <- coef(m_occ)
  d[i] <- d[i] + 1e-6
  (g19(d) - g19(coef(m_occ))) / 1e-6
})
se19 <- sqrt(drop(t(grad19) %*% vcov(m_occ) %*% grad19))
delta_ci <- occ19_hat + c(-1.96, 1.96) * se19

# the band, at the surveyed years, in the order students build it
years <- occ$elapsed
curves <- matrix(NA, nrow = 1000, ncol = length(years))
for (i in 1:1000) {
  curves[i, ] <- plogis(draws[i, "a"] + draws[i, "b"] * years)
}
lower <- apply(curves, 2, quantile, 0.025)
upper <- apply(curves, 2, quantile, 0.975)
obs <- occ$n_occupied / occ$n_routes
in_band <- sum(obs >= lower & obs <= upper)
band_w <- upper - lower

preds <- matrix(NA, nrow = 1000, ncol = length(years))
for (i in 1:1000) {
  p_i <- plogis(draws[i, "a"] + draws[i, "b"] * years)
  preds[i, ] <- rbinom(length(years), size = occ$n_routes, prob = p_i) / occ$n_routes
}
pred_lower <- apply(preds, 2, quantile, 0.025)
pred_upper <- apply(preds, 2, quantile, 0.975)
in_pred <- sum(obs >= pred_lower & obs <= pred_upper)
pred_w <- pred_upper - pred_lower

# Lecture 19's band: the same simulation with the parameters held at their estimates
set.seed(19)
p_fit <- plogis(a_hat + b_hat * years)
fake <- replicate(1000, rbinom(length(years), size = occ$n_routes, prob = p_fit) / occ$n_routes)
fixed_w <- apply(fake, 1, quantile, 0.975) - apply(fake, 1, quantile, 0.025)

# extrapolating: the curve out to 2035, for the figure
e_long <- seq(0, 38, by = 0.25)
long_curves <- sapply(1:1000, function(i){ plogis(draws[i, "a"] + draws[i, "b"] * e_long) })
long_band <- apply(long_curves, 1, quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
w2035 <- diff(long_band[, length(e_long)])

# counts against development, on the log scale
m_nb <- mle2(count ~ dnbinom(mu = exp(log_mu0 + b * frac_built), size = exp(log_k)),
             start = list(log_mu0 = 2.5, b = -3, log_k = 0), data = counts)
b_nb <- coef(m_nb)["b"]
ci_b_nb <- confint(m_nb)["b", ]
half_hat <- log(2) / -b_nb
half_ci <- log(2) / -ci_b_nb

set.seed(22)
draws_nb <- MASS::mvrnorm(1000, mu = coef(m_nb), Sigma = vcov(m_nb))
built <- seq(0, 0.5, by = 0.01)
counts_curves <- matrix(NA, nrow = 1000, ncol = length(built))
for (i in 1:1000) {
  counts_curves[i, ] <- exp(draws_nb[i, "log_mu0"] + draws_nb[i, "b"] * built)
}
nb_lower <- apply(counts_curves, 2, quantile, 0.025)
nb_upper <- apply(counts_curves, 2, quantile, 0.975)
half_recipe <- quantile(log(2) / -draws_nb[, "b"], c(0.025, 0.975))

mu_20 <- exp(draws_nb[, "log_mu0"] + draws_nb[, "b"] * 0.2)
mu_20_hat <- exp(coef(m_nb)["log_mu0"] + b_nb * 0.2)
mu_20_ci <- quantile(mu_20, c(0.025, 0.975))
one_route <- rnbinom(1000, mu = mu_20, size = exp(draws_nb[, "log_k"]))
one_route_ci <- quantile(one_route, c(0.025, 0.975))
n_above40 <- sum(counts$count > 40)
```

## Today's agenda {.smaller}

- Intervals on what the parameters **predict**: a value in one year, a change
  over time, a whole curve
- One recipe that works for all of them: **draw, compute, take the middle 95%**
- **Confidence** intervals versus **prediction** intervals

. . .

[Type and run]{.type-badge} on a code block: type it into your script and run it.
Code without the label is there to watch.

::: {.notes}
Bolker 7.5. Lecture 17 put intervals on parameters. Today puts them on the
things biologists actually report, which are almost never a single parameter.
Lecture 17 ended with a picture of a band around the occupancy curve and a
promise that Lecture 21 would draw it. This is that lecture.
:::

## The story so far {.smaller}

- A parameter's interval: every value within **1.92** of the best NLL (Lecture 17)
- We can compare models, and fit them reliably (Lectures 18 to 20)
- **Today:** intervals on what the fitted model **predicts**

::: {.notes}
Thirty seconds.
:::

## Get set up {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
library(bbmle)
library(biometrydata)

occ <- bobwhite_occupancy
counts <- bobwhite_counts

# occupancy against years since 1997, as in Lecture 17
m_occ <- mle2(n_occupied ~ dbinom(size = n_routes, prob = plogis(a + b * elapsed)),
              start = list(a = 2, b = -0.05), data = occ)
coef(m_occ)
confint(m_occ)
```
:::

**Check:** $a$ = `r round(a_hat, 2)` and $b$ = `r round(b_hat, 3)`, the decline of
about 6% a year in the odds of occupancy from Lecture 17.

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. The model they have fitted three times now, written with mle2's
formula interface from Lecture 18. a is the log odds of occupancy in 1997
(elapsed = 0), b the change in log odds per year.

confint() gives the profile intervals from Lecture 17. Leave them on screen:
the next few slides use them.
:::

# The question is rarely a parameter

## What biologists actually ask {.smaller}

| The question | The answer is | Uses |
|---|---|---|
| What fraction of routes had bobwhite in 2019? | $\text{logistic}(a + 22b)$ | $a$ and $b$ |
| How much did occupancy fall, 1997 to 2019? | $\text{logistic}(a) - \text{logistic}(a + 22b)$ | $a$ and $b$ |
| At what level of development are counts halved? | $\log(2) / -b$ | $b$ only |
| What does the whole decline look like? | $\text{logistic}(a + b \cdot \text{year})$, every year | $a$ and $b$ |

. . .

`confint()` gives intervals on $a$ and $b$. **None of these is $a$ or $b$.**

::: {.notes}
The motivation for the whole lecture. A manager does not want the log odds of
occupancy in 1997; they want to know how many routes still have bobwhite, and
how fast that is changing. Each of those numbers is calculated from the
parameters, and each needs its own interval.

The 22 is the number of years from 1997 to 2019, the last survey.
:::

## Occupancy in 2019, give or take what? {.smaller}

The estimate: $\text{logistic}(a + 22b)$ = **`r pct(occ19_hat)`** of routes.

. . .

A first idea: plug in the ends of the two intervals, every combination:

| $a$ | $b$ | Occupancy in 2019 |
|---|---|---|
| `r round(corners$a[1], 2)` (low) | `r round(corners$b[1], 3)` (low) | `r pct(corners$p19[1])` |
| `r round(corners$a[2], 2)` (high) | `r round(corners$b[1], 3)` (low) | `r pct(corners$p19[2])` |
| `r round(corners$a[1], 2)` (low) | `r round(corners$b[3], 3)` (high) | `r pct(corners$p19[3])` |
| `r round(corners$a[2], 2)` (high) | `r round(corners$b[3], 3)` (high) | `r pct(corners$p19[4])` |

. . .

So somewhere from `r pct(min(corners$p19))` to `r pct(max(corners$p19))`? **Too
wide, by a lot.**

::: {.notes}
Ask the room first: given the two intervals on screen, how would you get an
interval for occupancy in 2019? Someone will suggest this. It is a natural idea,
and it is what a lot of people do.

A range of `r round(100 * diff(range(corners$p19)))` points for one number is suspicious when each parameter is fairly
well pinned down. The next slide shows why.
:::

## Why the corners are wrong {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.85
#| fig-width: 7.6
par(mar = c(3.4, 4.6, 0.6, 0.6), mgp = c(2.2, 0.6, 0), las = 1)
plot(draws[, "a"], draws[, "b"], pch = 16, cex = 0.5, col = rgb(0.16, 0.48, 0.69, 0.35),
     xlim = range(c(draws[, "a"], ci_occ["a", ])) + c(-0.03, 0.03),
     ylim = range(c(draws[, "b"], ci_occ["b", ])) + c(-0.002, 0.002),
     xlab = "a (log odds of occupancy, 1997)", ylab = "", bty = "l")
title(ylab = "b (change per year)", line = 3.5)
rect(ci_occ["a", 1], ci_occ["b", 1], ci_occ["a", 2], ci_occ["b", 2], border = "grey30", lty = 2)
points(corners$a, corners$b, pch = 4, cex = 2.2, lwd = 3, col = "#b2182b")
points(a_hat, b_hat, pch = 16, cex = 1.4)
```

Each blue dot is a pair of values the data support. The dashed box is the two
intervals. **Two of the corners sit far from every dot.**

::: {.plain}
The ends of two intervals are rarely plausible together. Here, a higher start goes with a steeper decline.
:::

::: {.notes}
The correlation between a and b is `r round(cor_ab, 2)`: if 1997 occupancy was
a little higher than estimated, the decline must have been a little steeper to
end at the same 2019 values, and vice versa. The dots lie along a tilted
ellipse, and the box drawn from the two intervals is mostly empty space.

The two corners that set the extremes of the plug-in range, low a with low b
and high a with high b, go against that tilt. They are combinations the data
rule out, which is why the plug-in range was so wide.

This is the same correlation that made the slice overconfident in Lecture 17,
and that made the calendar-year model hard to fit in Lecture 20.

How the dots were made is the next section.
:::

# One recipe: draw, compute, summarize

## The recipe {.smaller}

1. **Draw** 1,000 plausible sets of parameters from the fit, the blue dots
2. **Compute** the number you care about from each set
3. Take the **middle 95%** of those 1,000 numbers

. . .

It works for **any** number you can calculate from the parameters: a value, a
difference, a ratio, a whole curve.

::: {.plain}
If you do not know the parameters exactly, try many plausible values and see how much the answer moves.
:::

::: {.notes}
Bolker calls this a population prediction interval, PPI, which is an unhelpful
name: it is a confidence interval, not a prediction interval in the sense of the
end of today. It is also close to what a Bayesian analysis does with its
posterior draws. Students do not need either label; "the recipe" is enough.

It is Lecture 13's simulation idea again: when the math is hard, simulate.
:::

## Where plausible values come from {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
vcov(m_occ)                 # the variance-covariance matrix
sqrt(diag(vcov(m_occ)))     # standard errors of a and b
cov2cor(vcov(m_occ))        # how strongly a and b move together
```
:::

| Part of `vcov()` | Means |
|---|---|
| the diagonal | how uncertain each parameter is: its **standard error**, squared |
| off the diagonal | how the two move **together** |

**Check:** standard errors `r round(se_occ["a"], 3)` and `r round(se_occ["b"], 4)`,
and a correlation of `r round(cor_ab, 2)`.

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. vcov() describes the shape of the bottom of the NLL bowl: how wide
it is in each direction, and which way it tilts. mle2 works it out from how
sharply the NLL curves at the bottom (the Hessian, for anyone who wants the
word).

The standard errors are the ones the plus-or-minus 1.96 SE shortcut from
Lecture 17 uses. That is the caveat for today's recipe: it treats the bowl as a
smooth, symmetric bowl, which is the shortcut's assumption. It is fine when the
parameters are on a scale where the bowl is round, which is one more reason to
fit on the logit or log scale, as we did here. It is not fine for a rare
species on the natural probability scale, Lecture 17's counterexample.
:::

## Step 1: draw {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
set.seed(21)
draws <- MASS::mvrnorm(1000, mu = coef(m_occ), Sigma = vcov(m_occ))
head(draws)
cor(draws)
```
:::

`mvrnorm()` draws from a **multivariate normal**: centered on the estimates, with
the spread and the tilt from `vcov()`.

**Check:** 1,000 rows, one plausible $(a, b)$ pair in each, and a correlation of
about `r round(cor(draws)[1, 2], 2)`, the tilt from the picture.

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. MASS comes with every R installation. MASS:: uses one function from
it without loading the whole package, which matters because loading MASS hides
dplyr's select(), a confusing error for anyone using the tidyverse.

Each row of draws is one blue dot from the corners picture. Point at the
correlation: rnorm() twice would have drawn a and b independently, filling the
whole box. mvrnorm() keeps the tilt.
:::

## Steps 2 and 3: compute, summarize {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
# occupancy in 2019 (22 years after 1997), once for each draw
occ19 <- plogis(draws[, "a"] + 22 * draws[, "b"])

hist(occ19)
quantile(occ19, c(0.025, 0.975))     # the middle 95%
```
:::

**Check:** `r pct1(occ19_ci[1])` to `r pct1(occ19_ci[2])` of routes. Your last
decimal may differ.

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. The calculation is the formula from the table, written once; R
applies it to all 1,000 rows at once. The histogram is the uncertainty in the
answer, and the quantiles cut off 2.5% at each end.

Compare with the plug-in corners: `r pct(min(corners$p19))` to
`r pct(max(corners$p19))`. The recipe's interval is about a third as wide,
because it never uses a pair of values the data rule out.
:::

## Two surprises {.smaller}

| Method | Occupancy in 2019 |
|---|---|
| plug in the corners | `r pct(min(corners$p19))` to `r pct(max(corners$p19))` |
| **the recipe** | **`r pct(occ19_ci[1])` to `r pct(occ19_ci[2])`** |

. . .

1. The recipe's interval is about **a third as wide**
2. The real 2019 survey found bobwhite on **52 of 71 routes, `r pct(obs19)`**:
   *outside* the interval

. . .

Is the model wrong? Hold that thought until the end of the lecture.

::: {.notes}
The second surprise is the setup for prediction intervals. Let someone guess.
The short answer, for later: this interval is about the model's average for
2019, the trend line. Any single year's survey scatters around that line, and
2019 happened to land above it.
:::

## Your turn: how much was lost? {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

**By how many percentage points did occupancy fall from 1997 to 2019?**

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
# occupancy in 1997, for every draw, goes here (hint: elapsed is 0 in 1997)

# the drop, for every draw, goes here (you already have occ19)

# the middle 95% of the drop goes here
```
:::

**Hint:** slide 13 computed occupancy in 2019 for every draw. Do the same for
1997, then subtract.

**Check:** a drop of about **`r round(100 * drop_hat)` points**, from
`r round(100 * drop_ci[1])` to `r round(100 * drop_ci[2])`.

::: {.notes}
Four minutes. Three lines:

occ97 <- plogis(draws[, "a"])
drop <- occ97 - occ19
quantile(drop, c(0.025, 0.975))

The point to draw out: the drop uses both parameters, and it is the kind of
number a report or a management plan would actually quote. No new method, just
a different formula in step 2. That is the strength of the recipe.
:::

## Two other ways, and when they work {.smaller}

| Method | Occupancy in 2019 | Works when |
|---|---|---|
| **the recipe** | `r pct1(occ19_ci[1])` to `r pct1(occ19_ci[2])` | always; the bowl should be roughly round |
| **rewrite the model** so the number is a parameter | `r pct1(rewrite_ci[1])` to `r pct1(rewrite_ci[2])` | you can rewrite it, one number at a time |
| the **delta method**, from slopes and `vcov()` | `r pct1(delta_ci[1])` to `r pct1(delta_ci[2])` | as for $\pm$ 1.96 SE |

. . .

Rewriting, for this model: measure time from 2019 instead of 1997. Then $a$ **is**
the log odds of occupancy in 2019, and `confint()` gives its profile interval.

::: {.notes}
Watch only. Three methods, one answer, to within a point.

Rewriting is Lecture 20's centering idea used on purpose: measure the covariate
from wherever you want a to mean something. The code, for anyone curious, is in
the solutions:

occ$from2019 <- occ$elapsed - 22, refit with from2019 in place of elapsed, and
plogis(confint(m_2019, parm = "a")).

It gives a profile interval, the most trustworthy kind, but it only works for
numbers you can turn into a parameter, and a curve would need one refit per year.

The delta method appears in many papers and in some R functions. It
approximates the uncertainty using the slope of the formula at the estimate. It
makes the same assumption as plus-or-minus 1.96 SE, so it fails where that
does. Bolker 7.5.2 has the details; students do not need to compute it.
:::

# A band around the curve

## From one year to every year {.smaller}

A curve is the same calculation at **every year**. So the band is the recipe, run
once per year:

- one **row** per draw (1,000)
- one **column** per year (`r length(years)`)
- the middle 95% of **each column**

::: {.notes}
The only new thing in the code coming up is bookkeeping: a matrix to hold a
whole curve for each draw, and apply() to summarize each column.
:::

## The band, step 1 {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
years <- occ$elapsed                 # the surveyed years, 0 to 22

# one row per draw, one column per year
curves <- matrix(NA, nrow = 1000, ncol = length(years))
for (i in 1:1000) {
  curves[i, ] <- plogis(draws[i, "a"] + draws[i, "b"] * years)
}

# the middle 95% of each column (the 2 means columns)
lower <- apply(curves, 2, quantile, 0.025)
upper <- apply(curves, 2, quantile, 0.975)
```
:::

**Check:** `dim(curves)` is 1000 by `r length(years)`. `lower[23]` and `upper[23]`
are 2019's interval from before.

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. Inside the loop, draws[i, "a"] is a single number and years is a
vector, so each pass computes a whole curve, all 23 years, for one draw.

apply(curves, 2, quantile, 0.025) reads as: for every column of curves, run
quantile(column, 0.025). The 2 means columns; a 1 would mean rows.
:::

## The band, step 2 {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
obs <- occ$n_occupied / occ$n_routes
plot(occ$year, obs, pch = 16, ylim = c(0.5, 1),
     xlab = "year", ylab = "fraction of routes occupied")

lines(occ$year, plogis(coef(m_occ)["a"] + coef(m_occ)["b"] * years), lwd = 2)
lines(occ$year, lower, lty = 2)
lines(occ$year, upper, lty = 2)
```
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.4
#| fig-width: 7
plot(occ$year, obs, pch = 16, ylim = c(0.5, 1),
     xlab = "year", ylab = "fraction occupied")
lines(occ$year, plogis(a_hat + b_hat * years), lwd = 2)
lines(occ$year, lower, lty = 2)
lines(occ$year, upper, lty = 2)
```

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. The plot is Lecture 19's "draw the fit", plus two dashed lines.
:::

## Why the band flares {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.8
#| fig-width: 7.6
par(mar = c(3.4, 3.4, 0.6, 0.6), mgp = c(2.1, 0.6, 0))
plot(occ$year, obs, pch = 16, xlim = c(1997, 2035), ylim = c(0.2, 1),
     xlab = "year", ylab = "fraction of routes occupied", bty = "l")
for (i in 1:40) {
  lines(1997 + e_long, long_curves[, i], col = rgb(0.16, 0.48, 0.69, 0.35))
}
lines(1997 + e_long, long_band[1, ], lty = 2, lwd = 2)
lines(1997 + e_long, long_band[2, ], lty = 2, lwd = 2)
abline(v = 2019.5, col = "grey50")
text(2020, 0.95, "no data past here", adj = 0, cex = 0.8, col = "grey30")
```

Forty of the 1,000 curves. They **pivot** near the middle of the data.

::: {.plain}
The band is narrowest where the data are, and keeps widening the further you predict beyond them.
:::

::: {.notes}
Within the data, the band is about `r round(100 * min(band_w))` points wide near
the middle and `r round(100 * band_w[23])` points wide in 2019. By 2035 it is
`r round(100 * w2035)` points wide, and that is the optimistic version: it
assumes the decline keeps the same logistic shape for sixteen more years, which
nothing in the data can tell us.

Like a seesaw: a small change in the slope barely moves the middle, and swings
the ends a long way. This is also why centering in Lecture 20 made a and b
nearly uncorrelated: the middle of the data is the pivot.
:::

## Is the model wrong? {.smaller}

Only **`r in_band` of the `r nrow(occ)`** years fall inside the band, 2019 among the
misses.

. . .

The band answers: **where is the trend line?**

It does not answer: **where will a year's survey land?** Each year's survey
scatters around the line: binomial scatter, from sampling 70-odd routes.

. . .

That needs a **prediction interval**.

::: {.notes}
Answer the "two surprises" cliffhanger here. The model is not wrong; the band
is answering a different question from the one the points pose. A confidence
band that contained 95% of the data points would be far too wide to say
anything about the trend.
:::

# Where will the next survey land?

## Confidence or prediction? {.smaller}

| Interval | Includes | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| **confidence** | uncertainty in the **parameters** | where is the average, the trend line? |
| **prediction** | the parameters **plus** the scatter of real data | where will one new observation land? |

. . .

To get a prediction interval: run the recipe, but in step 2 **simulate a survey**
from each draw, instead of computing its average.

::: {.plain}
A confidence interval says where the average is. A prediction interval says where the next observation will land, so it is always wider.
:::

::: {.notes}
An archery picture works: the confidence interval is where the center of the
target is; the prediction interval is where the next arrow lands.

The scatter is the distribution half of the model, from Lecture 17's "a model is
two things": the deterministic curve says where the average is, the
distribution says how data scatter around it. A confidence interval uses only
the first half; a prediction interval uses both.
:::

## The prediction interval {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
preds <- matrix(NA, nrow = 1000, ncol = length(years))
for (i in 1:1000) {
  p_i <- plogis(draws[i, "a"] + draws[i, "b"] * years)
  # one simulated survey per year, with that year's number of routes
  preds[i, ] <- rbinom(length(years), size = occ$n_routes, prob = p_i) / occ$n_routes
}
pred_lower <- apply(preds, 2, quantile, 0.025)
pred_upper <- apply(preds, 2, quantile, 0.975)

lines(occ$year, pred_lower, lty = 3, col = "red")
lines(occ$year, pred_upper, lty = 3, col = "red")
sum(obs >= pred_lower & obs <= pred_upper)
```
:::

**Check:** about **`r in_pred` of `r nrow(occ)`** years inside the red lines.

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. The loop is the band's loop with one added line: rbinom()
simulates a survey from each draw's curve.

This is Lecture 19's "simulate from the fit" with one improvement: there, every
fake survey used the single best-fit curve; here, each uses a different
plausible curve. That is the full prediction interval.
:::

## Both, together {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.1
#| fig-width: 7.6
par(mar = c(3.4, 3.4, 0.6, 0.6), mgp = c(2.1, 0.6, 0))
plot(occ$year, obs, pch = 16, ylim = c(0.45, 1), type = "n",
     xlab = "year", ylab = "fraction of routes occupied", bty = "l")
polygon(c(occ$year, rev(occ$year)), c(pred_lower, rev(pred_upper)),
        col = rgb(0.84, 0.38, 0.30, 0.18), border = NA)
polygon(c(occ$year, rev(occ$year)), c(lower, rev(upper)),
        col = rgb(0.16, 0.48, 0.69, 0.40), border = NA)
lines(occ$year, plogis(a_hat + b_hat * years), lwd = 2)
points(occ$year, obs, pch = 16)
legend("topright", c("confidence: the trend", "prediction: one year's survey"),
       fill = c(rgb(0.16, 0.48, 0.69, 0.40), rgb(0.84, 0.38, 0.30, 0.18)),
       border = NA, bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
```

The prediction band is about **`r round(mean(pred_w) / mean(band_w))` times as
wide**. Almost all of that width is the scatter of real surveys.

::: {.notes}
Lecture 19's band, with the parameters fixed at their estimates, averaged
`r round(100 * mean(fixed_w))` points wide; this one averages
`r round(100 * mean(pred_w))`. Parameter uncertainty adds very little: for
predicting one survey, the noise in the data dominates. For describing the
trend, it is the only thing that matters.

Which to report depends on the question. "Is bobwhite occupancy declining?" is
about the trend: confidence. "How many routes will have bobwhite next year?" is
about one observation: prediction.
:::

## Vote: confidence or prediction? {.smaller}

Hands up for **confidence**, then for **prediction**:

| | The question | |
|--|------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------|
| 1 | Has bobwhite occupancy declined since 1997? | [**confidence**]{.fragment} |
| 2 | Is the warbler you just caught unusually light? | [**prediction**]{.fragment} |
| 3 | How much does protection raise reef fish biomass, on average? | [**confidence**]{.fragment} |
| 4 | Seedlings to plant at a restoration site so 100 survive | [**prediction**]{.fragment} |
| 5 | Does a pesticide lower bumblebee colony survival? | [**confidence**]{.fragment} |
| 6 | Will the next reef you survey, at 15 m, have over 30 species? | [**prediction**]{.fragment} |

. . .

::: {.plain}
Ask: is the question about the average, or about one particular case? The average needs a confidence interval. One case needs a prediction interval.
:::

::: {.notes}
Five minutes. Read each question, take the two votes, then click to reveal the
answer before moving to the next. Ask one person from the losing side to say why
they voted that way; the wrong answers are usually reasonable, and saying why
they are wrong is what makes the distinction stick.

What to say about each:

1. A trend, the average change over years. Confidence. This is the band.
2. "Unusually light" means outside the range where individual birds of that
   species, at that wing length, normally fall: a range for one bird, not for
   the average bird. Prediction. With a confidence interval for the average
   weight, most healthy birds would look abnormal.
3. The average effect of protection across reefs, the quantity a comparison of
   protected and unprotected sites estimates. Confidence. The vote often splits
   here; contrast it with "will protecting THIS reef raise its biomass by 20%?",
   which is prediction.
4. One site's outcome, and the planting has to work at that site, not at the
   average site. Prediction, and the lower end matters most. Planting for the
   average survival rate would fall short at about half of sites.
5. An average effect across colonies, what a field or lab experiment estimates.
   Confidence.
6. One new survey. Prediction. It is the reef version of the landowner's route,
   coming up in a few minutes.

The pattern to draw out: the questions about one particular thing (a bird, a
site, a reef, a route) are the ones people most often answer with the wrong,
too-narrow interval. Using a confidence interval for a prediction question is
the common mistake, and it makes you overconfident, which in conservation can
mean a restoration that fails or a population that drops below a threshold no
one expected it to reach.
:::

# Your turn: bobwhite and development

## Get set up: counts and development {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
# bobwhite counted on a route, against the fraction of the route developed
m_nb <- mle2(count ~ dnbinom(mu = exp(log_mu0 + b * frac_built), size = exp(log_k)),
             start = list(log_mu0 = 2.5, b = -3, log_k = 0), data = counts)
coef(m_nb)

set.seed(22)
draws_nb <- MASS::mvrnorm(1000, mu = coef(m_nb), Sigma = vcov(m_nb))
```
:::

**Check:** $b$ = `r round(b_nb, 2)`.

Why `log_mu0` and `log_k`? Draws from a normal can be **negative**. On the log
scale, every draw is a legal value.

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. The model from Lecture 18's comparison of distributions. Fitting
on the log scale was Lecture 20's Fix 3, transforming. It matters twice over
here: drawing on the natural scale, some draws of k could come out negative,
and rnbinom() would fail. On the log scale, exp() of any draw is positive.
:::

## One parameter: transform the ends {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

The **halving point**: how developed a route can be before its expected count
halves. It uses $b$ **only**.

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
log(2) / -coef(m_nb)["b"]                  # the halving point
log(2) / -confint(m_nb)["b", ]        # its interval: transform the ends
```
:::

**Check:** `r pct(half_hat)` developed, from `r pct1(half_ci[1])` to
`r pct1(half_ci[2])`. The recipe gives `r pct1(half_recipe[1])` to
`r pct1(half_recipe[2])`.

::: {.plain}
When a number is calculated from just one parameter, put each end of that parameter's interval through the same calculation: the two answers are the number's interval. With two or more parameters, that runs into the corners problem from slide 8, so use the recipe.
:::

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. This is Lecture 17's back-transforming of endpoints, used for a
derived quantity. It works because the halving point depends on b alone and
moves in one direction as b changes: the most extreme plausible b gives the most
extreme plausible halving point.

The lower end comes from the steeper slope: a steeper decline halves the count
sooner.
:::

## Your turn: the band for development {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
built <- seq(0, 0.5, by = 0.01)     # 0% to 50% developed

counts_curves <- matrix(NA, nrow = 1000, ncol = length(built))
for (i in 1:1000) {
  # the expected count at every value of built, for draw i, goes here
}

# the lower and upper ends of the band go here

plot(counts$frac_built, counts$count, col = "grey", ylim = c(0, 40),
     xlab = "fraction developed", ylab = "bobwhite counted")
# the fitted curve and the two ends of the band go here
```
:::

**Hint:** slides 19 and 20 built the occupancy band. Same steps, with the draws
from slide 29 and `exp(log_mu0 + b * built)` in place of `plogis(a + b * years)`.

**Check:** at 20% developed (`built[21]`), the average route has
`r sprintf("%.1f", nb_lower[21])` to `r sprintf("%.1f", nb_upper[21])` bobwhite.

::: {.notes}
Eight minutes. Everything they need is on the occupancy slides; the changes are
the formula, exp(log_mu0 + b * built) instead of plogis(a + b * years), and the
names.

`r n_above40` of the 1,360 counts are above 40 and fall off the top of the plot;
the ylim keeps the band visible.

For anyone done early: the next slide.
:::

## Your turn: one route {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

A landowner's route is **20% developed**. How many bobwhite will its survey find?

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
mu_20 <- exp(draws_nb[, "log_mu0"] + draws_nb[, "b"] * 0.2)
quantile(mu_20, c(0.025, 0.975))          # the average route at 20%

# one simulated count per draw goes here (hint: rnbinom(), with mu = mu_20;
# for size, use the log_k column of draws_nb, the way mu_20 used log_mu0)

# the middle 95% of those counts goes here
```
:::

**Check:** the average route, `r sprintf("%.1f", mu_20_ci[1])` to
`r sprintf("%.1f", mu_20_ci[2])` birds. One route, **`r one_route_ci[1]` to
`r one_route_ci[2]`**.

::: {.notes}
Five minutes. The missing lines:

one_route <- rnbinom(1000, mu = mu_20, size = exp(draws_nb[, "log_k"]))
quantile(one_route, c(0.025, 0.975))

The contrast is the point of the lecture in one line: we know the average route
at 20% developed quite precisely, and still cannot say much about any one
route. Both statements are true, and they answer different questions. The
negative binomial's clumping, from habitat patchiness, is what makes the single
route so unpredictable.
:::

# Wrapping up

## Which tool, when {.smaller}

| You want an interval on | Use |
|---|---|
| one parameter | `confint()` (Lecture 17) |
| a number built from **one** parameter | `confint()`, then transform the ends |
| a number built from **several** | the recipe: draw, compute, middle 95% |
| a whole curve | the recipe, at every $x$ |
| where **new data** will land | the recipe, plus simulating the scatter |

Coming up: `lm()` and `glm()` have **shortcuts** for some of these (Lectures 23
and 24). The recipe works for any model, including the ones they cannot fit.

::: {.notes}
The slide to photograph. The last row is the prediction interval; every other
row is a confidence interval.

The shortcuts: predict() with interval = "confidence" or "prediction" for lm(),
and predict() with se.fit = TRUE for glm(), back-transformed. No need to show
them today; they are worth more once students can fit those models.

For Assignment 3, due Friday: a band around a fitted curve is a good way to
show the comparison between models, though it is not required.
:::
